findings.finding: A pool is a named routing target. Requests wait in it until an available worker claims them.
The agent loop (inference, planning) stays in Cursor's cloud. The worker only executes tool calls (terminal, file edits, browser). Pools change infrastructure ownership, not where the loop runs.
Team Pools are scoped to Enterprise teams.
Pool use cases include service account authentication instead of individual browser logins, and labels that route work by environment, team, repo or hardware.
Cursor-managed Cloud Agents are recommended for most teams, including those needing private network access, before taking on a worker fleet.
A worker opens one long-lived outbound HTTPS connection to Cursor's cloud. Tool calls are sent to the worker over that connection.
No inbound ports, public IPs or VPN tunnels are required. Artifacts (screenshots, videos) upload to Cursor.
Documented capacity limit is 200 workers per user and 1000 per team.
Admin dashboard toggles: Allow Self-Hosted Machines (opt in per run) and Require Self-Hosted Machines (routes every Cloud Agent run to self-hosted workers).
Pool workers need a service account API key.
Worker prerequisites are the agent CLI, git on PATH (needed for git remotes or --clone-git-repos), a workspace directory, and access to build tools and secrets.
Pool workers authenticate with a service account API key or a per-claim session token minted from it. User, personal, team and organization API keys cannot start pool workers.
The key can be passed as CURSOR_API_KEY or --api-key.
agent worker --pool [name] start registers for pool assignment. The name defaults to 'default'. Each Cloud Agent session claims one worker at a time.
--idle-release-timeout keeps the worker alive after a session ends to handle follow-up messages. Default is 3600 seconds.
--computer-use lets claimed agents click, type and screenshot. On macOS the first start installs a Cursor Computer Use helper that needs Accessibility and Screen Recording grants.
--worker-dir is repeatable up to 20 paths. The first root is the primary repo for assignment identity and dashboard display. Extra roots add no repositories to a request.
Git in extra roots uses credentials already on the worker. A minted GitHub token covers only the repos in the request.
Create An Agent takes one repo for the default pool or a repo-backed pool. Several repos go to an any-repo pool whose workers run --clone-git-repos.
'agent worker ... debug --json' is a preflight. Worker options go before start or debug.
The dashboard shows a worker under its primary repo only. No named multi-repo environment object exists in the portal. Verbose logs (workspacePaths, x-repository-urls) are the source of truth.
Pool mode allows one Cloud Agent claim at a time. Without --pool, shared assignment is allowed. --management-addr exposes /healthz, /readyz and /metrics.
Repo-backed pools carry a repo=<owner/repo> label. Any-repo pools match on pool name only and appear under 'Any repo'.
Any-repo workers need no git remote. A .cursor/rules/*.mdc with alwaysApply under the --worker-dir gives per-request repo instructions.

--clone-git-repos is opt-in, implies --mint-github-token, and needs team-admin enablement and git on PATH. It is valid only on any-repo named pools (not default, no repo= or name= binding, not My Machines).
Clean checkouts of a claimed repo are reused when origin matches (git 2.26+). Otherwise the worker clones beside it. Cloned repos are deleted when the claim ends. Reused checkouts are kept.
A failed clone leaves the request in the queue. Operators see a generic failure.
--clone-git-repos, --mint-github-token and --sync-dashboard-secrets assume one worker per container or OS user.

Agents start against any-repo pools with env.type 'pool' and env.name set to the pool name. repos can be omitted. Repos do not narrow worker selection. A Slack team or channel default any-repo pool lets @Cursor start without a resolved repo.

Pools are durable. They persist after the last worker disconnects, so capacity can scale to zero. A new --pool name creates the pool implicitly. Pools are managed through POST, GET and DELETE on /v0/private-workers/pools. DELETE is a soft delete and does not affect connected machines.
List Pools and pending requests are the intended signals for scale-up decisions.

--pool takes a name. CURSOR_WORKER_POOL_NAME sets it from the environment. --pool-name is a deprecated alias. Workers started without --pool are multi-use and belong to no pool. Sessions route only to workers registered with the selected pool name.

Pool requests match on labels: repo=<owner/repo> when a repo is given, pool=<name> for named pools. Pool workers handle Require-Self-Hosted runs (except worker=/machine= targets), self_hosted=true or sh=1, pool=<name>, and repo selection from trigger surfaces.

Slack, GitHub and Linear triggers use key=value options (self_hosted, sh, pool, worker, machine). Options inside code blocks are ignored. Invalid or valueless options stay in the prompt as text. Linear also supports pool labels for delegated issues. A pool= in the comment beats a label.
Policy differs by surface. Slack rejects opt-in when Allow is off. GitHub honors only repo OWNER and COLLABORATOR commenters. Linear posts an agent activity error when Allow is off.
The Cloud Agent API uses the same resolver with usePrivateWorker and labels fields.

Self-hosted workers run command-based hooks from the workspace .cursor/hooks.json, and on Enterprise from dashboard-managed hooks. --on-session-start and --on-session-end add commands without editing hooks.json.
Prompt-based hooks, Tab hooks and workspaceOpen do not run on workers. sessionStart and sessionEnd fire on claim and release and are skipped on Cursor-managed Cloud Agents.
sessionStart input lists repo_urls and repos (repo_url, primary, optional ref) so a hook can check out refs or repos the worker lacks.
Labels are key-value worker descriptors set by --label flags, a JSON file or a TOML file (starts at 362). The shown span ends before the TOML example. Lines 365-409 were read by a prior reader.

Required outbound hosts include api2.cursor.sh and api2direct.cursor.sh for the agent session, downloads.cursor.com for CLI updates and Computer Use install, and cloud-agent-artifacts.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com for artifacts.
HTTPS_PROXY or https_proxy configures proxy use.
Blocking api2 hosts stops the worker from starting or continuing a session. Blocking the artifact bucket only breaks artifact surfaces.

The Kubernetes operator and WorkerDeployment chart are deprecated. The recommended path is anysphere/k8s-workers, with the worker controller using --spawn and optionally --warm-idle. No CRD is required. Other hosts and partner platforms are listed under Integrations.

'agent worker controller --spawn <path>' runs a hook once after a claim, or once per missing warm worker. Flags: --api-key, --pool (repeatable), --all-pools, --warm-idle, --session-token, --repository, --endpoint.

Claim-then-spawn is the default mode. It lists pending requests, watches the SSE stream and claims each request. Warm mode keeps N idle workers per pool, never claims, and reconciles against GET /v0/private-workers/pools every 60 seconds. There is no spawn lease, so concurrent warm controllers can over-spawn.

With --session-token the hook receives a per-claim session token (CURSOR_AUTH_TOKEN, expiry in CURSOR_AUTH_TOKEN_EXPIRES_AT) instead of the API key. It serves one claim, ends with the claim or on key deletion or expiry (7-day backstop), and can be replaced through Create A Session Token. Warm workers still receive the API key.

After a session ends the worker stays connected for --idle-release-timeout (default 1 hour, env CURSOR_WORKER_IDLE_RELEASE_TIMEOUT) waiting for follow-ups. A follow-up resets the timer. On timeout the CLI exits with code 0. 0 disables idle release. The Release-a-claim API frees the worker at once and is refused while a turn is using it.
After a timeout Cursor marks the worker freed. A restarted chat reconnects to a fresh machine and does not keep workspace state unless the pool uses hibernation.

Hibernation uses a pool-level workerReadyTimeoutSeconds (default 0, set via POST /v0/private-workers/pools). A follow-up for an offline claimed machine is advertised as a claimed_offline entry carrying claimedWorkerId and wakeTimeoutMs. The controller restores a snapshot and starts a worker with the same CURSOR_AGENT_WORKER_ID. If it cannot, it releases the claim. Otherwise the claim lapses and a fresh created entry is advertised. Snapshot timing keys off worker exit code 0 or Get An Agent status IDLE.

A custom controller watches the queue, claims and starts workers. It authenticates only with the pool service account key (Basic or Bearer). Queue monitoring is a list plus an SSE stream (GET /v0/private-workers/pending-requests and /stream) with streamCursor. Cursors expire after 5 minutes and the stream returns 410 Gone. Events (created, claimed_offline, claimed, expired) are hints. The list is the source of truth.

Additional endpoints: list workers (status and scope filters, limit 1-100), list pools (connectedWorkerCount, inUseWorkerCount, isStale), worker summary, get worker, POST claim (with optional sessionToken true), POST tokens, POST claims/{id}/release (HTTP 400 'Worker in use' during a turn, and a second claim is rejected while a live claim exists), and POST claims/{id}/fail (message up to 500 chars, valid only while the agent is ACTIVE and a turn is waiting).

A management server (--management-addr) exposes /metrics, /healthz and /readyz. Gauges: connected, session_active, last_activity. Counters: connect_attempts, connect_retry, session_ends with reason (stream_end, stream_error, session_closed, session_error, connection_timeout, session_aborted). The reasons mention HTTP/2 sessions.
Only model file chunks and artifacts leave the network. Workers connect outbound over HTTPS. Privacy Mode is respected. Each agent session gets a dedicated worker.
Other API key types are rejected. Admins see all workers. Members see only their assigned workers.

CLI reference flags: --worker-dir, --label, --labels-file, --idle-release-timeout, --computer-use, --display, --share-desktop, --pool, --single-use (legacy), --pool-name, --api-key, --auth-token, --auth-token-file (re-read on reconnect so a controller can rotate tokens), --clone-git-repos, --mint-github-token, --sync-dashboard-secrets (team-admin Secret sync), --on-session-start/end, --identity-socket (per-claim OIDC token socket, CURSOR_AGENT_SOCKET), --worker-id (env CURSOR_AGENT_WORKER_ID) and -e/--endpoint (default https://api2.cursor.sh).
Worker sizing follows CI runner or devbox sizing for the served repo. No fixed spec exists.
Project-level skills in .cursor/skills/ or .agents/skills/ load automatically on workers. Personal skill sync applies to managed Cloud Agents, not self-hosted workers.

The FAQ says MCP servers work on self-hosted workers, are configured through the Cloud Agents dashboard, and are routed by transport type. The routing table itself sits at 387-396, outside the spans read here. This span names no specific transport.
Workers run project and enterprise hooks. A pool worker serves one agent at a time.
Mac pool workers can run computer use via --computer-use. Screen Recording cannot be granted by MDM silently, so approve it once on the template image.
